# Searching by file type

When you search a project with ripgrep, you usually don't want every file.
You want the Python files, or you want everything except the generated
JavaScript bundles. ripgrep already knows the difference: it ships with a
built-in list of file types, each one a name attached to the glob patterns
that identify it. Four flags let you use, extend and inspect that list:
`--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add` and `--type-list`.

## `--type`: search only this kind of file

`-t`/`--type` limits ripgrep to files matching the type you name. Say you're
in ripgrep's own source tree and want every place that calls `fn run`, but
only in Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

or, more succinctly, with the short flag and the type name run together:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

A type is just a name for one or more glob patterns. `rust` means `*.rs`.
`python` means `*.py` and `*.pyi`. Some types cover more ground than a
single extension: `c` matches both `*.c` and `*.h`, so `--type c` catches
source and header files in one flag, where a hand-written glob would need
`-g '*.{c,h}'`.

You can give `--type` more than once. Each one adds to the set of types
you're willing to search, so `-trust -tpython` searches Rust *and* Python
files, not their intersection.

`--type` also accepts the special value `all`, which behaves as if you'd
passed `--type` for every type ripgrep knows about, including any you've
defined with `--type-add`. That sounds like it should be the same as no
filtering at all, but it isn't: plain `rg pattern` searches everything that
isn't ignored, while `--type all` searches only files matching *some*
recognized type. A shell script with no extension is invisible to `--type
all`, even though `--type sh` exists, because nothing in the `sh` type's
globs matches an extensionless filename.

Worth knowing before you rely on `--type`: it has lower precedence than
both `--glob`/`-g` and anything in your ignore files. If a `.gitignore`
excludes a file, `--type` won't bring it back.

## `--type-not`: search everything except this kind

`-T`/`--type-not` is the mirror image. It removes a type instead of
selecting one:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
```

or

```
$ rg clap -Trust
```

In short, `-t` means "include files of this type," `-T` means "exclude
files of this type." You can give `--type-not` more than once, and mix
`-t` and `-T` in the same command to include some types while excluding
others.

`--type-not` understands `all` too, and inverted: `--type-not all` searches
only files that ripgrep doesn't recognize as any type at all. So in a
directory holding `my-shell-library.bash` (matched by the `sh` type) and a
bare `my-shell-script` (matched by nothing, since it has no extension),
`--type all` finds matches only in the `.bash` file, and `--type-not all`
finds matches only in the extensionless one.

## `--type-list`: see what's available

Before searching by type, it helps to know what types exist and what each
one matches. `--type-list` prints them:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each line is a type name, a colon, and a comma-separated list of the globs
behind it. The full list is long, so you'll usually want to narrow it.
Piping the output through ripgrep itself works well:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^rust:'
rust: *.rs
```

`--type-list` takes into account any types you've added or cleared earlier
on the same command line, so it's also how you confirm a custom type you
just defined looks the way you expect.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

ripgrep's built-in types cover well-known formats, but you'll eventually
want one of your own. Say you regularly search "web" files: a mix of HTML,
CSS and JavaScript with no single built-in type. `--type-add` defines one,
using brace expansion to fold three globs into one:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines `web` as `*.html`, `*.css` and `*.js` combined, then
immediately searches it for `title`. Give `--type-add` several times if
you'd rather add globs one at a time; each one adds to what's already
defined for that type, built in or your own, rather than replacing it. Run
`--type-add` with `--type-list` instead of a search to check what you've
built:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
```

`web` shows up even though it isn't one of ripgrep's built-in types.

`--type-add` can also build a type from other types, with the `include`
directive. This defines `src` as everything the `cpp`, `py` and `md` types
match, combined:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

You can still add more globs to `src` afterward with another `--type-add`.
Type names are limited to Unicode letters and numbers; punctuation isn't
allowed.

One catch: `--type-add` only affects the command it's given on. It saves
nothing, so retyping it gets old fast. Two ways around that. A shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

Or a line in your ripgrep configuration file, the file named by the
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

Either way, `-tweb` is then available in every search without redefining
it. (A companion flag, `--type-clear TYPE`, handles the rarer case of
throwing out a type's existing globs to start over, rather than adding to
them.)

None of these four flags touch what's on disk. They only decide which
files ripgrep looks at for the one command you run them on; nothing is
remembered afterward unless you put it in an alias or a configuration file
yourself.
